scope: Weights are authored per-building priors, not census percentages: dwelling/household counts, structural material categories and photographed examples cannot directly measure footprint frequencies or pigment shares. regions.scope: Inspected Malana roofscape and Kalpa street; both mountain samples differ from low foothill towns and the dry Spiti valley. State urban slabs are retained from inventory instead of a universal timber chalet.

evidence.title: Government2011 household roof-material baseline
evidence.note: Dated comparative construction inventory; not a current color-frequency or building count.

weight_basis.construction: 2011 roofconcrete44.7%, stone/slate37.4%, sheets12.0%. Recent Kalpa image and older Malana view show metal replacement roofs among slate and concrete. Urban slabs and rural stone/timber/render stay mixed.
weight_basis.finishes: Actual gray slate, silver/brown/red/green metal and pale render/stone/dark timber are visible. The Malana image is strongly processed: color families are retained at restrained saturation and its extreme warmth is not sampled literally.

visual_references.scope: Photographer’s2025 Kalpa residential street view
visual_references.observed: Gray rough slate roofs, exposed stone with painted blue timber joinery, white plaster at lower stories, brown/silver sheet roofs and concrete infill nearby.

visual_references.scope: Photographer’s2016 Malana village roofscape
visual_references.observed: Green/red/silver and weathered metal mixed with slate; plaster, stone and timber houses. Image is strongly color-processed: it establishes pigment families, not calibrated saturation.

label: Province-specific tile, sheet and timber housing
character: Ordinary plastered masonry and timber-board houses have strongly regional roof-covering mixtures. Java tile traditions, Sumatra sheet roofs, Kalimantan timber stock and eastern-island sheet housing are explicit census-backed province recipes.
scope: BPS Long Form Population Census housing tables, collected in 2022, cover provincial urban/rural households. Thirty-three atlas-matched province records retain the material differences; five provinces have inspected housing photographs, the others remain stock-reviewed with paint prevalence unresolved. Current atlas boundaries predate some new province splits. No ceremonial roof or temple form is used as the national house prior.

evidence.title: BPS 2022 predominant roof covering table
evidence.scope: National and province urban/rural household counts
evidence.note: Ceramic/genteng, metal/seng, asbestos sheet, concrete and wooden/other coverings are separate census categories. Shape alone cannot distinguish ceramic from metal tile; unknown other coverings are not automatically thatch.

evidence.title: BPS 2022 predominant visible wall table
evidence.scope: National and province urban/rural household counts
evidence.note: Masonry, plastered bamboo/wire, wood boards/logs and other coverings are separate. Rendered masonry in the reviewed ordinary photographs is represented by plaster; structural concrete does not mean exposed stone.

evidence.title: Government SiKumbang technical listing and photograph
evidence.note: The roof specification explicitly distinguishes colored metal tiles from the light steel framing. Batako walls are visibly plastered and gray.

weight_basis.construction: Form weights approximate the separately tabulated wall and roof marginals; they are not a measured joint distribution or building-footprint census. Concrete roofs are assigned to masonry; the remaining identified roofs are divided between masonry and timber using wall shares. Small categories below 0.3% are omitted. Plastered bamboo and unspecified other walls/roofs remain unresolved, rather than being falsely called earth, timber, thatch or masonry. This limitation is particularly substantial in East Nusa Tenggara and rural Papua. Metropolitan apartment household counts also do not equal rooftop counts.
weight_basis.finishes: Six inspected reference groups establish cream, gray, yellow and green plaster, natural vertical timber, dark red/brown ceramic, colored corrugated and stamped-metal sheets. Province-specific photo palettes have explicit scope. Other provinces inherit this limited observed material palette with unresolved local paint prevalence; stock-reviewed is not visual approval. Census asbestos is approximated by the matte-sheet appearance, with no claim to identifying chemistry from a photograph.

The listings distinguish ceramic tile from multiroof/metal tile instead of inferring chemistry from color.

visual_references.scope: Ministry housing-program photograph reproduced by Kompas: Central Java

visual_references.scope: SiKumbang developer photograph reproduced by detik: Padang house and neighbor
visual_references.observed: Cream/white plastered masonry, a green neighboring facade, white joinery and red stamped-metal roofing. Published house specifications identify colored zinc/sheet roofs; the rolled shape is not evidence of ceramic.

visual_references.scope: Ministry PUPR photograph reproduced by Medcom: South Kalimantan BSPS house
visual_references.observed: Unpainted honey-brown vertical timber boards and posts, darker upper gable, timber joinery, corrugated sheet underside and a slightly raised wooden porch. This is an actual modest completed house rather than an ornate ceremonial building.

visual_references.scope: Ministry PUPR published Papua 2021 program photograph
visual_references.observed: Green painted smooth wall panels, red-brown joinery, blue corrugated roof and blue corrugated gable panel; natural timber roof posts. Structural wall chemistry is not inferred from green paint. It establishes contemporary infill, not all highland housing.

visual_references.scope: Government SiKumbang listing: completed Puri Mas Atambua example, Belu
visual_references.observed: Gray plaster over batako block, red accent columns, white trim, brown door and red tile-stamped metal roof. Technical specification explicitly identifies colored metal tile covering and a light steel frame; it is not clay tile.

label: Brick and pale-stone urban facades, earth terraces and Caspian pitched housing
character: Contemporary brick, pale cut-stone facing and plastered concrete/masonry dominate the urban prior. Earthen terrace fabric remains an explicit older-stock alternative; the Caspian provinces have independently specified metal, tile and shingle-roof housing.
scope: Actual Tehran apartment, Yazd residential aerial and two Caspian household/village photographs supplement dated primary field descriptions by Christian Bromberger and earthquake engineers Mehrain/Naeim. No current national material-frequency census was verified, so all joint form weights are qualitative and scoped. Four province recipes replace a nationwide desert-house assumption; other provinces require finer evidence.

evidence.scope: Gilan plain, piedmont and mountain settlements
evidence.note: Documents distinct vernacular stocks and replacement of timber/thatch by block walls and galvanized sheet roofs; arid southern districts also have flat earthen or brick roofs. It is a dated field synthesis, not current paint-frequency data.

weight_basis.construction: The broad contemporary prior retains flat masonry/concrete and visible brick/stone-facing alternatives; surviving adobe receives a separate earthen archetype. Caspian pitch forms are not multiplied nationwide. Shares are authored interpretations of sampled stocks, with no numeric census claim.
weight_basis.finishes: Warm brick, pale rectangular stone facing, cream/gray plaster and ochre earth are physically distinct roles. Regional pigment/covering pairs come from inspected photographs. Roof equipment and shadows do not determine base color; no uniform beige palette or assumed blue slate.

visual_references.scope: Seller’s occupied Oraj/Aghdasieh apartment building, Tehran
visual_references.observed: Warm red-brown thin brick and pale cream rectangular stone-facing panels, white window frames and balcony rails, pale rendered balcony recesses. Stone facing is not evidence that the apartment frame is load-bearing stone.

visual_references.scope: Hanif Sadr family photograph reproduced by KQED; Gilan/Mazandaran border farm
visual_references.observed: Weathered pale plaster, dark natural timber posts and joinery, broad pitched roof covered by small boards and many ballast stones. Material identification is qualified: the coarse boards agree with regional shingle field descriptions; stones are ballast, not a claim of slate roofing.

visual_references.scope: Majid Sanaye photograph of occupied Shah Milarzan village, Gilan
visual_references.observed: Pale plaster, turquoise/blue and pink wall patches, blue timber joinery; red rolled ceramic, silver and rust-brown sheet roofs, and a matte gray corrugated replacement roof. Individual houses combine replacement roofs, so no one covering is universal. Photographer attribution retained in the original image.

visual_references.scope: Ahmad Lari House restoration foundation’s aerial showing surrounding Yazd residential fabric
visual_references.observed: Sand and light earth-colored courtyard houses with flat terraces and some low vaults, pale newer infill, roof-mounted equipment and shaded blue-gray patches. Monumental domes, windcatchers and the exceptional restoration house do not supply ordinary dwelling geometry; shadows are not blue pigment.

character: Light rendered/panel apartments contrast with brick-and-tile low-rise housing. Muted gray and warm clay coverings remain alternatives rather than one uniform capital-city style.
scope: Historical firsthand construction evidence is limited and not a current housing survey. Conservative modern neutral finishes avoid invented nationwide colour shares. Authored sRGB alternatives are art interpretation, not measured colours or statistical shares. Material roles include minority stock; existing subdivision and local profiles remain more specific. Render forms represent plastered concrete/block or coated masonry; brick/stone palette availability alone does not infer an exposed masonry façade.

label: White rendered modern terraces with pale masonry neighbors

scope: Actual contractor aerial photographs of 32 completed two-storey Al Amerat houses and the surrounding neighborhood in Muscat. character: Rendered town masonry coexists with earth and timber rural wall roles; sheet roofing and thatch remain distinct alternatives, without treating every mapped house as a traditional circular shelter.

Render forms represent plastered concrete/block or coated masonry; brick/stone palette availability alone does not infer an exposed masonry façade.

label: Modern rendered concrete and masonry housing
character: Modern concrete and coated masonry are the national ordinary-stock prior. Historic Najdi earth, Hijazi coral/lime and southwestern stone traditions require their own geographically scoped entries, rather than a fixed rural earthen-house share.
scope: 2024 Saudi-household construction evidence corrects the national structural prior, not roof color. Non-Saudi household stock and regional visible finishes remain incompletely audited. Existing broad pale pigments remain provisional until actual ordinary-house photo review; the cited Jeddah heritage source alone does not establish nationwide construction shares.

evidence.note: UNESCO Historic Jeddah: coral-stone houses with timber projecting architectural elements.

evidence.title: GASTAT Housing Statistics 2024
evidence.note: Reinforced concrete accounts for 90.0%, block/brick 9.7%, other 0.3%; apartments 45.0% and villas 31.0%. Structural categories are not visible finishes or roof coverings, and exclude non-Saudi-headed households.

urban.label: rendered concrete or block apartment and villa

weight_basis.construction: 2024 GASTAT establishes modern concrete/block dominance among Saudi households. Removed the unsupported equal-four rural mix and arbitrary earthen quota. One national construction prior is used until regional alternatives are explicitly substantiated; this is not a claim that every Saudi dwelling is identical.
weight_basis.finishes: Pending ordinary-house visual review. Existing pale wall and terrace colors are provisional, not measurements derived from structural census categories.

label: Cement-built terraces and sheet-roof compounds, with measured regional differences
character: White, cream, sand and gray coated masonry; predominantly flat concrete urban roofs and gray sheet-covered town/rural roofs, with geographically concentrated earth and thatch stock.
scope: National fallback for ordinary contemporary housing. Cement wall census categories describe construction, not necessarily exposed gray surfaces. Roof counts describe households in their main dwelling, not building polygons; priors are deliberately rounded art interpretations. Regional overrides separate Dakar and southern sheet-roof stock. Rural finish frequency and eastern village photography remain incomplete; this entry is stock-reviewed, not visually approved. Existing mapped roof shape, roof material, use and geometry retain ownership.

evidence.note: National cement walls 77.6%, cement with tile 12.6%; concrete roofs 44.6%, sheet 36.1%, tile/slate 8%, thatch 6.6%. Urban concrete 63.2% versus rural 12.7%; rural sheet 55.8%, thatch 15.7%. These are household shares, not exact procedural-building weights.
